A water softener is a household water treatment system that removes the minerals responsible for hard water, mainly calcium and magnesium.
Hard water is common in many homes. Although it is generally safe to drink, it can cause mineral buildup in plumbing, appliances, showers, and faucets.
A water softener helps reduce these problems by making the water softer.

 1. Softer skin and hair – Reduces mineral residue that can leave skin feeling dry and hair feeling dull or stiff.
2. Cleaner dishes and glassware – Helps prevent white spots, cloudy glasses, and mineral deposits.
3. Less soap and detergent – Soap lathers better in soft water, so you may use less laundry detergent, shampoo, and dish soap.
4. Longer appliance lifespan – Helps prevent scale buildup in dishwashers, washing machines, water heaters, and other water-using appliances.
5. Improved water heater efficiency – Reduces mineral buildup that can make water heaters work harder and use more energy.
6. Cleaner plumbing pipes – Helps prevent calcium and magnesium scale from accumulating inside pipes.
7. Softer, brighter laundry – Clothes can feel less stiff and may retain their color and softness better.
8. Less cleaning around the house – Reduces hard-water spots and crusty buildup on faucets, showerheads, tubs, and sinks.
9. Better shower experience – Helps soap and shampoo rinse away more easily.
10. Potential long-term savings – Less scale buildup can mean fewer appliance repairs, less cleaning, and reduced soap usage.

Verified all connections are tight and make sure all breaker sizes are within spec of the conductor ethic control. One major thing I didn’t notice is that there is a good amount of corrosion forming on the main neutral lug, as well as a little bit on the ground and neutral bar. I was informed that a lot of water and moisture tends to sleep through the walls in the basement which could be a possibility of where this is coming from. I also noticed that the exterior service is over 30 years old, which that could be the cause behind that as well. I did open up the meter base and only noticed little corrosion. However, the service wire goes under a roof for the balcony which is not convenient or up to code due to personnel being able to grab a hold of the conductor with the connections. Inform the homeowner that we are not 100% positive of where that corrosion for the panel is coming from but due to the age and location of the exterior service, I recommended replacing it with a service mast riser, which will go straight up from the meter base through the roof.. Power company will need to be contacted to run a new line from our service mast to the transformer. Inform the homeowner that replacing the service does not guarantee a fix to the corrosion but it is definitely highly recommended to replace. The only other thing I noticed during today’s evaluation is that the gas and water system is not properly bonded/grounded. A number for copper wire is required to go from the main electrical panel to the water meter, as well as the gas manifold to protect people from any shriveled shock on any gas, appliance or water fixture. I provide a option to replace the service which includes the grounding and bonding as well as a separate option for the grounding and bonding. All other electrical components are at the home or up to code and tested properly today. Emailed invoices and estimates to the homeowner.I completed the annual electrical system evaluation, beginning at the main electrical panel. Voltage readings were within acceptable ranges, all electrical connections were checked for proper tightness, and breaker sizes were verified to ensure they were appropriately rated for the connected conductors.

During the inspection, I discovered a noticeable amount of corrosion forming on the main neutral lug, along with minor corrosion on the neutral and grounding bars. Although the electrical system is currently operating and voltage readings are acceptable, continued corrosion can eventually compromise electrical connections and potentially lead to intermittent power loss, flickering lights, and other electrical distribution issues.

The exact source of the corrosion could not be determined during today’s evaluation. The homeowner mentioned that water and moisture have historically seeped through the basement walls, which could potentially contribute to the issue. Additionally, the exterior electrical service is over 30 years old, and its age and existing installation conditions may also be contributing factors.

I inspected the meter base and observed only minor corrosion in that location. However, I also identified concerns with the existing exterior service installation. The service conductors currently run underneath the balcony roof, leaving portions of the wiring and connections accessible to individuals. This installation is not ideal from a safety and code-compliance standpoint.

Due to the age and configuration of the existing exterior service, I highly recommend replacing it with a new service mast and riser. The proposed installation would extend vertically from the meter base, through the roof, providing a more appropriate and protected route for the service conductors. The utility company will also need to be contacted to coordinate running a new service line from the transformer to the newly installed service mast.

Important: Replacing the exterior electrical service does not guarantee that the corrosion currently present inside the main electrical panel will be eliminated. We cannot confirm the exact source of the corrosion at this time. However, given the age and condition of the existing service, replacement is strongly recommended as a preventative safety measure and to address the concerns with the current installation.

Another issue identified during today’s evaluation involves the home’s grounding and bonding system. The existing gas and water systems are not properly bonded to the electrical grounding system. Proper bonding conductors need to be installed from the main electrical panel to the water service piping and gas manifold. This bonding is essential to help prevent dangerous voltage differences and reduce the risk of electrical shock when touching plumbing fixtures or gas appliances.

I provided the homeowner with two separate options:

1. Complete Service Replacement: Includes replacement of the exterior electrical service with a new service mast and riser, along with the necessary grounding and bonding improvements.
2. Grounding and Bonding Only: Addresses the deficiencies in the existing grounding and bonding system without replacing the exterior electrical service.

All other electrical components evaluated throughout the home were found to be operating properly and were tested within acceptable parameters at the time of today’s inspection.

Invoices and estimates outlining the recommended work and available options were emailed to the homeowner for review and consideration.

LPH arrived to begin the annual electrical system check. Upon arrival, no immediate electrical concerns were presented prior to our electrical inspection. 

We began our evaluation at the main electrical/distribution panel. This is where we assessed the internal conditions, age, connections and voltage readings. During this inspection, all of the inspected parameters meet the required threshold for a healthy panel. However, there are a few recommendations we assessed during this inspection. 

First we discovered that there two sets of breakers that are apart of a shared neutral circuit. A specific type of breaker would need to be installed in their place to properly protect this circuit and any personnel who needs to work on this circuit. Lastly, there’s no system put in place to protect appliances/electronics from spikes of electric which target the sensitive components inside these units. A whole home surge protection device is recommended if the homeowners were interested in  protecting their main utility equipment with a one time investment unit.

Next, we inspected all of the protective systems for personnel and equipment in the home such as the smoke detectors, GFI protection devices, and the grounding system. First, we discovered that the water and gas meter does not meet today’s grounding standards to protect against any leakage of electricity from traveling on the pipes. The next was confirmation that all of the existing smoke detectors and carbon monoxide detectors are up-to-date. However, we identified two bedroom locations that do not have active smoke detectors. Lastly, we identified two junction boxes that do not have the any covers installed and two sets of open splices that have been taped for the lighting above the workshop area. All other devices in the home were tested and functioning properly prior to leaving today.

We provided options to remedy all of our electrical recommendations, which was presented today. All of the options that were not approved will be emailed along with the electrical evaluation form and invoice for today’s visit. We thank you for allowing us in your home to service you and we look forward to servicing you in the future.

e.438328499:
As we approach the winter months and the start of flu season, maintaining healthy indoor air quality becomes increasingly important. With windows and doors remaining closed more frequently and heating systems running regularly, airborne particles and other contaminants can circulate throughout your home.

LPH recommends considering the following indoor air quality upgrades to help improve air filtration, reduce certain airborne contaminants, and support a cleaner, healthier indoor environment.

1. UV Air Purification Light

A UV air purification light is installed within your home’s HVAC system and uses ultraviolet light technology to help reduce certain airborne microorganisms as air circulates through the system. This technology can help support improved indoor air quality and provide an additional layer of protection against certain biological contaminants.

2. Electric Air Cleaner with Upgraded Filtration

An electric air cleaner with upgraded filtration is designed to capture airborne particles, including dust, pollen, and other common indoor particulates. By enhancing your HVAC system’s filtration capabilities, this upgrade can help improve indoor air quality, reduce particle circulation, and keep internal HVAC components cleaner.

Why Consider These Upgrades?

During the heating season, your HVAC system plays an important role in circulating and filtering the air throughout your home. Improving your system’s air purification and filtration capabilities can provide several benefits:

* Help reduce certain airborne contaminants and microorganisms.
* Capture more airborne particles, including dust and pollen.
* Support cleaner air circulation throughout your home.
* Help keep HVAC system components cleaner.
* Improve overall indoor comfort and air quality.

Prepare Your Home for the Winter Season

LPH encourages homeowners to explore these indoor air quality solutions before the heating season gets underway. Investing in enhanced air purification and filtration can be a proactive step toward maintaining a cleaner and more comfortable home environment throughout the winter months.

For more information about these upgrades and to determine which option may be best suited for your home’s HVAC system, contact LPH. We’re happy to help you make an informed decision about your indoor air quality needs.

e.439866585:
A spin-down sediment filter is designed to capture larger particles such as sand, silt, rust, and debris before they enter the home’s plumbing system. Unlike disposable cartridge filters, a spin-down filter uses a reusable stainless steel mesh screen that can be flushed clean by opening a purge valve, making maintenance quick and cost-effective.

The filter is typically installed on the main water line immediately after the water service enters the home and before other water treatment equipment, such as a water softener, iron filter, UV system, or water heater. Installing a spin-down filter helps protect plumbing fixtures and appliances from sediment buildup, extends the life of downstream filtration equipment, and reduces maintenance on water treatment systems.

The filter should be mounted where there is adequate clearance for servicing, and a drain or bucket should be available for periodic flushing. Routine maintenance involves opening the flush valve for several seconds to remove accumulated sediment, helping ensure reliable water flow and continued protection of the home’s plumbing system.

The existing well pump system is not equipped with a constant pressure switch. Due to the size of the home and the potential demand on the well system, the technician recommends installing a constant pressure switch to help maintain consistent water pressure throughout the home. This system would regulate the well pump to maintain a target pressure of approximately 60 PSI, helping provide more consistent water pressure when multiple plumbing fixtures are in use. Maintaining stable operating pressure can also help reduce unnecessary cycling of the well pump, potentially extending the life of the pump and improving the overall performance of the well system.

The homeowner has been experiencing ongoing sediment issues with the existing well water system and would like to add additional filtration to help address the problem. It is recommended to install a 20-inch sediment filter downstream of the spin-down filter. The spin-down filter will help capture larger particles and debris before the water reaches the 20-inch sediment filter, allowing the finer filter to capture smaller sediment particles. This two-stage filtration setup will help reduce sediment entering the home’s plumbing system, protect plumbing fixtures and water-using appliances, and improve overall water quality.

The well water was tested and showed a pH of 6.2, 1 grain per gallon (GPG) of hardness, and 2.5 ppm of iron. The low pH indicates acidic water, while the elevated iron level can contribute to staining, discoloration, and buildup throughout the home’s plumbing system and fixtures.

It is recommended to install a Sanitizer Plus water treatment system to help improve overall water quality. This system would help raise and stabilize the pH, provide additional treatment for the water, and reduce iron levels to help minimize staining and iron buildup. Correcting these water quality conditions can also help protect plumbing fixtures, appliances, and piping from the effects of acidic water and excess iron.

The treatment system would be installed on the main water supply near the pressure tank and water heater. Proper drainage and electrical connections will be required for the system to operate and regenerate as designed.

The last GFI, that is apart of the lamp post circuit is functioning correctly. However, in addition to most of these GFI’s either not functioning or being very old and slow to respond, they’re missing the proper exterior covers require required to protect against weather elements.  All other devices in the home were tested and functioning properly prior to leaving today.

We provided options to remedy all of our electrical recommendations, which was presented today. i.337165841:
During today’s electrical system check, LPH performed an evaluation of the home’s electrical system, including the electrical panel, breakers, internal connections, switches, receptacles, and accessible electrical devices throughout the home. We also evaluated the condition of the existing devices, checked for loose connections, signs of overheating, electrical arcing, physical damage, and general wear and deterioration. Exterior electrical devices and their protection against weather exposure and moisture intrusion were also reviewed.

During our inspection, LPH identified significant deterioration among the existing switches and receptacles. These devices are approximately 30 years old and have reached a point where multiple devices are showing signs of failure. We found cracked plastic housings, weakened connections, wiring slipping out of devices, and evidence of electrical arcing. Almost every electrical box we opened and inspected showed some degree of deterioration or connection concerns.

Before making any recommendations, we went over our findings directly with the homeowners and physically showed them the damaged devices and the conditions we discovered during the inspection. We explained how these devices deteriorate over time, why loose connections and electrical arcing are concerning, and the potential for overheating and electrical failure if these conditions are allowed to continue.

Recommendations & Options Reviewed With Homeowners:

1. Whole-Home Device Restoration: LPH recommended replacing all switches and receptacles throughout the home. Since these devices were installed around the same time, the widespread deterioration indicates that similar issues can reasonably be expected in devices that have not yet been inspected or are not currently showing symptoms. Replacing everything together provides a comprehensive restoration rather than waiting for individual devices to fail. This option also includes a dimmer switch and two GFCI receptacles as an added value.
2. Partial Home Device Replacement: An alternative option was provided to replace up to 50 switches and receptacles, allowing the homeowners to prioritize the most deteriorated devices while addressing a significant portion of the identified concerns.
3. Exterior Device & Weatherproofing Upgrades: As part of the device replacement options, LPH also included upgrading applicable exterior receptacles to weather-resistant devices, installing two weather-resistant GFCI receptacles, adding exterior in-use bubble covers to protect receptacles from direct rain and moisture exposure, and sealing exterior electrical enclosures with silicone to help prevent water intrusion.

We explained the importance of addressing these conditions proactively, especially considering the age of the devices and the widespread deterioration already identified. Continuing to operate with damaged devices and compromised connections increases the potential for additional arcing, overheating, and electrical failures.

At this time, the homeowners will be sent the estimates along with today’s electrical system evaluation for their review and consideration. They can take the time to review the available options and determine how they would like to proceed.

Thank you for allowing LPH into your home. It was a pleasure meeting with you, and we appreciate the opportunity to evaluate your electrical system.

e.438612387:
LPH recommends replacing all switches and receptacles throughout the home. During today’s inspection, we found that the existing devices are approximately 30 years old and have deteriorated significantly from normal use and age. Multiple devices were found with cracked plastic housings, weakened wire connections, and wiring beginning to slip out of the devices. Evidence of electrical arcing was also identified.

After inspecting multiple locations throughout the home, it became apparent that these issues are not isolated to one or two devices. Nearly every electrical box inspected showed some degree of deterioration or connection concerns.

Because these devices were all installed around the same time, it is reasonable to expect similar wear throughout the remainder of the home, including locations that have not yet shown obvious symptoms. Continuing to operate with deteriorating devices increases the potential for electrical arcing, overheating, and eventual electrical failure.

LPH strongly recommends proactively replacing all switches and receptacles throughout the home rather than addressing individual failures as they occur. This provides the homeowner with refreshed, secure electrical connections throughout the home and helps reduce the risk of future connection-related issues.

As an added value with this upgrade, LPH will include one dimmer switch and two GFCI receptacles at no additional charge.

Premium Whole-Home Surge Protection
LPH will install a premium whole-home surge protection device at the home’s main electrical panel. This device is designed to protect the home’s electrical system and connected equipment from damaging voltage spikes and transient surges before they can travel throughout the home’s wiring.
Many homeowners think of lightning when they hear the term “surge,” but the majority of power surges actually originate inside the home. Everyday appliances such as air conditioners, refrigerators, heat pumps, furnaces, microwaves, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and even garage door openers create small electrical surges—known as microsurges—every time their motors cycle on and off. While each individual surge is small, thousands of these microsurges occur over time and gradually wear down the sensitive electronic components found in today’s modern appliances and equipment.
Whole-home surge protection helps absorb and divert these surges away from the home’s electrical system, reducing cumulative damage to expensive electronics and appliances. This is especially important in newer homes, where nearly every major appliance contains sophisticated circuit boards and microprocessors that are far more sensitive to voltage fluctuations than older equipment.
In addition to protecting against internally generated microsurges, whole-home surge protection also provides a critical first line of defense against larger surges originating from the utility company, switching events on the electrical grid, nearby lightning strikes, or power being restored after an outage.
Benefits of premium whole-home surge protection include:
	• Protects HVAC systems, refrigerators, ovens, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and other major appliances.
	• Helps safeguard sensitive electronics such as televisions, computers, gaming systems, networking equipment, and smart home devices.
	• Reduces the long-term effects of everyday microsurges that slowly degrade electronic components.
	• Can help extend the service life of modern appliances and equipment by reducing electrical stress on internal circuit boards.
	• Helps minimize the likelihood of costly repairs or premature equipment replacement due to surge damage.
	• Provides continuous protection for the entire home’s electrical system without relying solely on individual plug-in surge strips.
	• Offers added peace of mind during storms, utility switching events, and unexpected power outages.
As homes continue to rely on more connected technology and electronically controlled appliances, whole-home surge protection has become one of the most valuable upgrades for preserving the reliability, longevity, and performance of a home’s electrical equipment.

Premium Surge Protection Warranty & Replacement Coverage

The installed surge protection device also provides additional protection beyond the device itself. If the surge protector is ever sacrificed or fails as a result of a covered surge event, the device is backed by a lifetime warranty and coverage of up to $100,000 toward covered damage to the home’s electrical components and connected equipment, subject to the manufacturer’s warranty terms and conditions.

If the surge protector ever needs to be replaced under the warranty, the replacement device is provided at no charge. LPH will also handle the replacement installation for a $150 labor charge, helping make future warranty replacement straightforward and affordable for the homeowner.

This means the homeowner is not simply purchasing a surge protector—they are adding a long-term layer of protection to the home’s electrical system while also having manufacturer-backed coverage in the event of a significant surge.

As homes continue to rely on more connected technology and electronically controlled appliances, whole-home surge protection has become one of the most valuable upgrades for preserving the reliability, longevity, and performance of a home’s electrical equipment.

i.339779140:
LPH returned today to complete the recommended electrical service replacement following the previous evaluation, which identified extensive water intrusion, corrosion, and moisture-related deterioration throughout the existing exterior meter base and interior electrical panel.

The existing water-affected service equipment was removed and replaced with a new electrical service assembly. This included installation of a new exterior meter base, emergency disconnect, conduit, and associated service wiring. New four-wire conductors were installed between the exterior disconnect and interior panel, allowing the interior panel to be properly reconfigured as a subpanel with the required separation of neutrals and grounds. The grounding and bonding systems were also addressed as part of the replacement, including the required bonding bridge and grounding connections.

All new grounding connections were established at the new exterior emergency disconnect. The existing grounding conductors were relocated from the interior panel to the new service disconnect, where the grounding system is now properly established. An additional grounding connection was also installed to the home’s metal water piping, providing the necessary supplementary grounding and bonding required by applicable electrical code.

A new 42-space Eaton CH electrical loadcenter was installed to replace the existing moisture-damaged panel. All existing branch-circuit wiring was properly relocated and terminated into the new panel. The entire panel was fully identified and relabeled to provide accurate circuit identification for the homeowners and for future electrical servicing.

Whole-home surge protection was also installed to provide an additional layer of protection against damaging voltage surges and electrical spikes that can affect appliances, electronics, and other sensitive equipment throughout the home.

As an additional measure to help prevent future water intrusion, the entire new service assembly was carefully sealed. All areas where electrical wiring, conduit, or other piping enter the home were fully sealed with silicone, along with the appropriate service entry points and exterior equipment connections. This helps close potential pathways for water to enter the home and protects the newly installed electrical equipment from exposure to outside moisture.

New weather-resistant exterior receptacles were also installed at both the front and back porches. The back porch receptacle was equipped with a new extra-duty in-use bubble cover to provide protection while the receptacle is being used and exposed to the elements. The existing cover at the front porch was inspected and remains code-compliant due to the protection provided by the porch overhang, so it was left in place.

Upon completion, all work was thoroughly inspected and tested. The new service equipment, panel, breakers, grounding and bonding connections, surge protection, and installed receptacles were tested and confirmed to be functioning properly. The electrical system was verified to be operating as intended before leaving.

Warranty Information: The newly installed service equipment is backed by a 10-year parts and labor warranty while the homeowners remain active members of the LPH Service Partner Plan.

Today’s invoice summary will be emailed to the homeowners for their records. Thank you for allowing LPH into your home. It was a pleasure working with you, and we look forward to servicing you again in the future!

i.339921329: This morning I arrived at the customers home to conduct their first annual electrical system check since their move in 2 months ago. Upon performing a thorough evaluation of the homes main electrical service I found no major discrepancies, however I had one substantial estimate for the homeowners at the time of our check today. The one recommendation I had was regarding the main breaker panel. The panel appears to be in the end stages of progressive corrosion. I analyzed substantial rust on not only the panel housing but some segments of wiring as well. Most of the panels bare copper/ aluminum exhibit signs of oxidization or corrosion from moisture exposure over the span of 50+ years.  The panel has eclipsed what we would deem to be the average life expectancy for breaker panels. The panel is 50 years old now. As panels age, the safety features within their breakers can begin to fail to function in the event of an electrical fault. We lose the ability to be able to gauge proper function of these breakers as they age until sometimes, we lose power entirely. Separate from this, should any breakers fail, or need to be replaced, it can be difficult to find replacements as they do not manufacture these parts anymore. Primarily the main breakers are the cause of concern. If the main breaker were to trip for any reason, there is a strong likelihood it would not reset, as it is not considered a “serviceable” breaker. The rest of the homes equipment appears to be in good condition with no other signs of potential failure. For all of the reasons listed above, I have provided a sole estimate today to replace the main breaker panel. Should you have any questions or concerns regarding todays visit or our findings, please do not hesitate to contact us. Thank you for having me out today and I look forward to our next visit!

During today’s electrical system check, LPH performed a thorough evaluation of the home’s electrical system. This included inspecting the main electrical panel, checking breakers for proper seating and signs of wear or overheating, inspecting accessible wiring and connections, and evaluating receptacles, switches, and GFCI protection throughout the home. We also checked the operation of the ceiling fan and its remote control system to identify any issues affecting normal operation.

During the evaluation, LPH identified several items that required attention:

* Electrical Panel: (2) existing 20-amp breakers were found to be noticeably loose and outdated. Loose breaker connections can create poor electrical contact, potentially leading to arcing, excessive heat buildup, and damage to the panel. Replacement was recommended to restore secure connections and reliable circuit protection.
* Interior Receptacles: (3) duplex receptacles were identified for replacement. One had loose backstab wire connections, while two others had worn internal contacts that were no longer maintaining proper contact with the neutral prongs of plugged-in devices. These conditions can lead to intermittent operation, poor electrical connections, and potential overheating.
* Kitchen GFCI: (1) kitchen GFCI receptacle had a physically deteriorating face with portions beginning to crack off. The homeowner also reported issues with the device tripping. Replacement was recommended to restore dependable operation and GFCI protection.
* Ceiling Fan: The existing ceiling fan remote receiver assembly required replacement to restore reliable communication between the remote and fan.

LPH reviewed the findings and recommendations with the homeowner, and all of the above-listed work was approved, completed, and tested today. The two 20-amp breakers, three duplex receptacles, kitchen GFCI receptacle, and ceiling fan remote receiver assembly were replaced.

All completed work was tested, and proper operation was verified prior to leaving the home.

Today’s electrical system check evaluation and invoice summary will be emailed to the homeowner for their records.

Thank you for choosing LPH and allowing us the opportunity to service your home. We appreciate your business!

Call Description: 

LPH recommends replacing the three existing Cutler-Hammer arc-fault breakers due to excessive heat buildup and extensive carbon dust accumulation on the electrical panel cover. These conditions are concerning and may indicate internal deterioration of the breakers, which can compromise their ability to operate safely and reliably. Given their age and current condition, replacement is recommended to restore dependable circuit protection and reduce the risk of continued overheating.

We also recommend installing whole-home surge protection at the main electrical service. Transient voltage spikes can occur from utility fluctuations, lightning activity, and everyday operation of electrical equipment throughout the home. Over time, these voltage spikes can contribute to premature wear of sensitive electronic components within appliances, LED lighting drivers, and other household electronics. The homeowner has experienced premature LED bulb failures and flickering throughout the home, which may be consistent with electrical component degradation. While these symptoms can have multiple causes, whole-home surge protection provides an added layer of defense against damaging voltage surges and helps protect the home’s electrical devices and appliances from avoidable damage.

Additionally, LPH recommends replacing the existing rear porch receptacle with a weather-resistant GFCI receptacle and installing an extra-duty, in-use bubble cover. The current gray cover cannot close while the awning remains plugged in, leaving the receptacle vulnerable to moisture and water intrusion. The recommended cover will allow the receptacle to remain protected from the elements while the awning is connected, helping reduce the risk of corrosion, nuisance tripping, and premature receptacle failure.

LPH will also install the outdoor light fixtures supplied by the homeowner, ensuring the new fixtures are properly connected and tested for operation.

These recommendations are intended to improve electrical safety, provide additional protection for sensitive electronics, and address the existing outdoor receptacle’s exposure to moisture.

LPH will rewire the unfinished basement and install six new dedicated circuits from the existing basement subpanel. This upgrade will provide properly distributed electrical service for the basement’s current and planned uses, reduce the electrical load on the existing circuits, and provide the appropriate protection for the new receptacles and connected equipment.

Basement Rewiring – Six New Circuits

1. Dedicated 15-Amp Radon Fan Circuit

* Install one new 15-amp circuit dedicated to the radon fan.
* Install a single receptacle at the designated location, with conduit piped down the wall to provide a protected wiring method.

This dedicated circuit will provide a separate power source for the radon fan rather than relying on a shared circuit serving other basement equipment and receptacles.

2. Dedicated 20-Amp Exercise Area Circuit

* Install one new 20-amp circuit to supply the basement exercise area.
* Install three receptacles to accommodate the designated exercise equipment.
* Install two receptacles along the wall bordering the mechanical room.
* Reuse the existing conduit at the designated location, remove the existing receptacle wiring, and install new wiring and a new receptacle.

Providing a dedicated circuit for the exercise area will help accommodate the electrical demand of the equipment without adding additional loads to the general basement receptacle circuit.

3. Dedicated 20-Amp Basement Kitchenette Circuit

* Install one new 20-amp circuit to supply the planned basement kitchenette.
* Install two receptacle locations at the designated areas.
* Pick up the upstairs kitchen island receptacle as part of this circuit using wiring accessible from the basement.

Including the upstairs kitchen island receptacle on this new circuit will help remove its load from the existing circuit serving the basement lighting, screened-in porch, and existing exterior receptacles. This will help distribute the electrical demand more appropriately and reduce the likelihood of nuisance tripping on the existing circuit.

This circuit will provide a separate power source for the kitchenette and kitchen island receptacles, helping distribute the electrical load as the basement living space is developed.

4. Dedicated 20-Amp Fireplace Heater Circuit

* Install one new 20-amp circuit dedicated to the basement fireplace heater.
* Install one receptacle at the designated location, with conduit piped down the wall.

A dedicated circuit will help accommodate the heater’s electrical demand without unnecessarily loading the general-purpose basement receptacle circuit.

5. Dedicated 20-Amp Exterior Hot Tub Circuit

* Install one new 20-amp circuit from the basement subpanel, routed across the basement and drilled through the exterior wall to the back porch.
* Install one weather-resistant GFCI receptacle with an appropriate in-use bubble cover to supply the 120-volt inflatable hot tub.

Because this receptacle will serve equipment used around water, proper ground-fault protection is particularly important. GFCI protection is designed to quickly interrupt power when an electrical fault creates a potentially dangerous shock hazard.

The final circuit and receptacle arrangement will need to meet the hot tub manufacturer’s electrical requirements and applicable code requirements for the installation location.

6. Dedicated 20-Amp General Basement Receptacle Circuit

* Install one new 20-amp circuit to supply the remaining designated basement receptacles.
* Reuse the existing conduit at one location and install a new receptacle.
* Cut in one receptacle along the stairway wall.
* Install three additional receptacles at the designated locations, using conduit down the block walls as needed.

This additional circuit will provide convenient receptacle access throughout the basement while distributing the electrical demand across multiple circuits instead of continuing to rely on the existing overloaded arrangement.

Basement Circuit Protection

The six new circuits will be installed from the existing basement subpanel using the appropriate wiring methods and circuit protection for their intended applications. The estimate includes:

* Four 20-amp dual-function AFCI/GFCI circuit breakers.
* One 20-amp AFCI circuit breaker.
* One 15-amp AFCI circuit breaker.

AFCI protection is designed to detect certain dangerous electrical arcing conditions that can lead to fires. GFCI protection helps reduce the risk of electrical shock by detecting ground faults and interrupting power. Dual-function breakers combine both protective features in one device.

The specified breakers will provide the intended protection for the new circuits while helping bring the installation into compliance with applicable electrical code requirements.

Existing Basement Wiring – Junction Box Transition

Currently, one existing circuit supplies the basement lighting and receptacles, exterior receptacles, screened-in porch receptacles, and kitchen island receptacle. This places a substantial number of electrical loads on a single circuit and can contribute to nuisance tripping when multiple devices are operating.

As part of this project, LPH will disconnect and transition the existing basement wiring as necessary, installing accessible junction boxes along the basement ceiling to maintain continuity for the existing circuits. This will allow the existing wiring to remain operational while the new circuits take over the designated basement receptacle loads and the upstairs kitchen island receptacle is transferred to the new kitchenette circuit.

The goal is to distribute the electrical demand more appropriately, reduce the burden on the existing circuit, and provide a more functional electrical layout for the basement and the home’s connected areas.

Whole-Home Surge Protection Recommendation

With the installation of multiple new circuits and sensitive AFCI/GFCI protective devices, LPH recommends adding a whole-home surge protector at the main electrical panel.

Modern electrical equipment, appliances, and electronic circuit boards can be damaged by voltage surges originating from utility disturbances, lightning-related events, or electrical equipment cycling on and off within the home. These events can also contribute to premature wear or damage to sensitive electronic components.

A whole-home surge protector provides an additional layer of defense by helping divert damaging transient voltage away from the home’s electrical system and connected equipment. It is particularly beneficial for homes with modern appliances, HVAC equipment, electronics, and other sensitive devices.

Although surge protection cannot prevent every type of electrical disturbance or guarantee that equipment will never be damaged, it is a worthwhile protective upgrade for the home.

Additional 20-Amp Exterior Circuit From the Main Panel

LPH will install one additional 20-amp circuit from the main electrical panel to supply two receptacles serving the main garage area: one receptacle inside the garage below the electrical panel and one exterior receptacle on the opposite side of the wall.

This installation will include:

* Routing the new circuit from the main panel and dropping down the wall to the designated locations.
* Installing a GFCI-protected receptacle at the designated exterior location.
* Installing one receptacle inside the garage below the electrical panel.
* Providing convenient power sources for both interior garage and exterior use.
* Providing a more suitable power source for the garage microwave, reducing reliance on the existing garage door opener receptacle and extension cord.

Currently, the microwave is being powered through the garage door opener receptacle using an extension cord. This is not an ideal arrangement for an appliance that draws substantial current, particularly when the circuit may already be supplying other equipment. A properly installed receptacle on a new circuit will provide a more appropriate power source and help reduce nuisance tripping caused by shared electrical loads.

Exterior Receptacle Repairs and Weather Protection

LPH will also address the damaged exterior receptacles by replacing the existing devices with new weather-resistant receptacles and providing the required GFCI protection.

This portion of the work includes:

* Two weather-resistant GFCI receptacles.
* Two weather-resistant duplex receptacles.
* Reuse of the existing boxes and appropriate bubble covers where suitable.

Weather-resistant receptacles are designed to better withstand outdoor environmental exposure. Combined with appropriate GFCI protection and suitable covers, these replacements will help reduce the risk of moisture-related deterioration, electrical faults, and shock hazards.

The existing boxes are already equipped with appropriate bubble covers, so the existing covers will be retained where they are in suitable condition and compatible with the new receptacles.

Additional Grounding and Bonding Improvements

LPH recommends completing the home’s grounding and bonding system by installing a grounding clamp on the existing metal water line and adding approximately 5 feet of grounding conductor to bond the home’s gas piping system as required by applicable electrical code.

* Water Line Grounding: Install an approved grounding clamp on the existing metal water line and connect it to the home’s grounding electrode system as appropriate. This will address the incomplete grounding arrangement and help establish the required electrical connection to the metal water piping where applicable.
* Gas Line Bonding: Install approximately 5 feet of additional grounding conductor to properly bond the home’s gas piping system to the electrical grounding system, as required by applicable code provisions.

Proper grounding and bonding help provide a safe, intentional path for fault current, allowing protective devices to operate as intended during an electrical fault. These connections also help reduce dangerous voltage differences between metal piping systems and other grounded electrical components.

Completing these improvements will help bring the home’s grounding and bonding system into compliance with applicable electrical code requirements and provide an additional layer of protection for the home’s occupants and electrical equipment.

Installation, Testing, and Completion

All new circuits will be routed from the designated electrical panels using appropriate wiring methods, conduit, junction boxes, and circuit protection for their intended applications. LPH will complete the installation in accordance with applicable electrical code requirements, verify the new connections, and test the installed devices and circuits for proper operation.

The overall goal of this project is to provide a safer, more organized, and more functional electrical system for the unfinished basement and surrounding areas. By adding dedicated circuits for the radon fan, exercise equipment, kitchenette, fireplace heater, and hot tub, transferring the upstairs kitchen island receptacle to the new kitchenette circuit, expanding general receptacle capacity, and addressing the exterior electrical concerns, LPH will help accommodate the home’s electrical needs while reducing dependence on the existing heavily loaded circuit.

LPH will replace the existing expired smoke detectors throughout the home with new smoke detectors equipped with 10-year sealed lithium battery power. This upgrade will provide the homeowner with reliable smoke detection while eliminating the need for routine battery replacements over the detectors’ service life. All new detectors will be properly installed and tested to verify operation, helping maintain dependable early-warning protection for the home and its occupants.

LPH recommends replacing the existing 34-year-old Crouse-Hinds electrical panel with a brand-new 42-space Eaton CH electrical panel while retaining the home’s existing 200-amp service capacity.

Although the existing Crouse-Hinds panel is rated for 200 amps, its age and original design make replacement a worthwhile investment in the home’s electrical safety, reliability, and ability to accommodate modern electrical demands. Electrical panels are responsible for distributing power throughout the home and providing overcurrent protection to individual circuits. As panels age, breakers and internal connection points can experience wear, deterioration, and reduced reliability. Breaker connections on the bus bar can also loosen over time, potentially causing overheating, arcing, or unreliable circuit operation.

Why Upgrade the Existing Panel?

1. Aging Electrical Equipment

At approximately 34 years old, the existing Crouse-Hinds panel has provided decades of service. However, its age warrants consideration of replacement before deterioration or component failures create a more urgent situation. Replacing the panel allows LPH to install new equipment rather than continuing to depend on aging internal components and connections.

2. Better Support for Today’s Electrical Demands

Modern homes typically place greater demands on their electrical systems than they did decades ago. Today’s households rely on larger appliances, home office equipment, entertainment systems, exercise equipment, electronic devices, and other electrical loads that may not have been anticipated when the original panel was installed.

The existing panel’s 200-amp rating does not automatically mean the home needs a larger service. However, replacing the older panel provides an opportunity to improve circuit organization, evaluate the home’s electrical distribution, and accommodate additional circuit protection and future electrical projects where capacity permits.

3. Upgrade to a New 42-Space Eaton CH Panel

LPH will replace the existing Crouse-Hinds panel with a new 42-space Eaton CH panel. This provides a modern panel assembly with additional circuit spaces to help organize the home’s electrical system and accommodate future circuit additions, subject to the available service and load capacity.

The new panel will also provide a suitable platform for compatible circuit breakers and modern protective devices as needed for the home’s electrical requirements.

4. Improved Long-Term Reliability and Serviceability

Replacing the existing panel allows LPH to evaluate the incoming service conductors, grounding and bonding connections, neutral and ground terminations, and branch-circuit connections as part of the installation. This includes inspecting the breaker connections at the bus bar for looseness, signs of overheating, or other conditions that may affect safe operation. This helps identify concerns that may otherwise remain hidden within aging equipment.

A new panel can also make future electrical maintenance and troubleshooting more straightforward by providing current, compatible equipment and a more organized circuit layout.

5. Opportunity to Incorporate Whole-Home Surge Protection

As part of the panel replacement, LPH recommends installing whole-home surge protection to help protect sensitive electronics and appliances from damaging voltage transients originating from utility disturbances, lightning-related events, and electrical equipment cycling within the home.

Modern appliances and electronic equipment contain circuit boards and sensitive components that can be vulnerable to voltage surges. Whole-home surge protection provides an additional layer of defense for the home’s electrical system and connected equipment.

Scope of Work

LPH will:

* Remove the existing 34-year-old Crouse-Hinds electrical panel.
* Install a new 42-space Eaton CH electrical panel while maintaining the existing 200-amp service rating, provided the existing service components and installation support that configuration.
* Transfer the existing branch circuits to the new panel using compatible circuit breakers and appropriate wiring methods.
* Inspect breaker connections at the bus bar and address any loose, damaged, or overheated connections identified during the installation.
* Inspect and address grounding, bonding, neutral, and equipment grounding connections as required for the installation.
* Verify circuit identification and organize the panel directory.
* Evaluate the existing service connections and associated components for any additional concerns identified during replacement.
* Test the completed installation to verify proper operation.
* Provide whole-home surge protection as a recommended additional upgrade, if included in the approved scope.

The Long-Term Benefit

Replacing the existing Crouse-Hinds panel is a proactive investment in the home’s electrical infrastructure. Rather than waiting for aging equipment to develop a problem, the homeowner can move forward with a modern panel that offers additional circuit spaces, improved serviceability, and a better foundation for future electrical upgrades.

The goal is not simply to replace a panel because it is old. It is to update an aging, critical electrical component so the home’s distribution system is better positioned to serve the family’s current needs and future electrical demands.

i.346220609:
This afternoon I arrived at the Drazdowski family home to conduct their annual electrical system and safety check. Upon performing a thorough evaluation of the homes main electrical service I found no major discrepancies. However, I did note that the panel has reached what we would consider to be the “average life expectancy” of a breaker panel. 

What this means in essence is that we can no longer truly guarantee proper function of the panel currently in the home. While I didn’t note any obvious signs of corrosion, burning, or melting of any of the internal components, which is ideal, the age of the equipment is still evident. Slight discoloration of the busbar due to years of heat build up from the electricity, and some spotting rust throughout are easily seen. Secondarily, when these panels increase in age, the probability of breakers proper function is dwindled, meaning they may begin to trip unnecessarily, or not trip at all. Unfortunately there is not really any way to anticipate, monitor, to predict when internal failures may or may not happen, so we choose to trust, and rely heavily upon the age of the equipment. 

It is also almost always encouraged to consider the age of the power supply feeding your panel, and conversely the home. Upon inspecting the homes exterior meterbase I once again found no major discrepancies, but years of shade have deposited a heavy layer of moss and natural growth on the susceptible rubber protective layer on the cable itself. while I didn’t see any obvious cracking or deterioration, it is almost guaranteed that there are failure points that may allow moisture to be deposited within the cable. This moisture can follow the wire all the way into the panel and end up corroding those fragile internal components if left unaddressed. Not to mention, the panel brand itself “Challenger” has an extensive history of premature failures, although this exact product happens to be there best and final iteration prior to shutting their doors for good. 

All in all, the panel appears to be in OK conditon but I still felt it wise to provide estimates to replace both the breaker panel, as well as the external portion as a means of preventing future failures. For all of the reasons listed above, I have provided two options today, the first to replace the breaker panel itself, and secondarily to replace the homes entire main electrical service comprising of both the panel, as well as the external meterbase and wiring.

Thank you for sharing your home with me this afternoon and I greatly look forward to our next visit. If you have any questions or concerns, please do not hesitate to contact us. Take care!

i.346844615:
LPH arrived to begin the annual electrical system check. Upon arrival, Matt had both a concern and electrical question prior to our inspection. First, Matt mentioned his concern with the switch in his bedroom that sparked and immediately stopped functioning after. We did a thorough evaluation, identifying that the switch itself needs to be replaced along with the switch adjacent to it that is broken. We also identified that both of the switches contained the plug-in/backstab style connections that create more heat and eventually cause more damage to the devices than the other wiring method. Matt’s question was installing a new switch for his decorative light fixture on the stair wall. We did a thorough scope of work and identified a outlet directly underneath this light that we use as a power source. 

We began our evaluation at the main electrical/distribution panel. This is where we assessed the internal conditions, age, connections and voltage readings. During this inspection, all of the inspected parameters meet the required threshold for a healthy panel.

We discovered that there’s no system put in place to protect appliances/electronics from spikes of electric which target the sensitive components inside these units. A whole home surge protection device is recommended if the homeowners were interested in  protecting their main utility equipment with a one time investment unit. This main electrical/distribution panel is also maxed out and most newer circuit or electrical equipment could not be installed within this existing panel

Next, we inspected all of the protective systems for personnel and equipment in the home such as the smoke detectors, GFI protection devices, and the grounding system. First, we discovered that the water and gas meter does not meet today’s grounding standards to protect against any leakage of electricity from traveling on the pipes. The next was confirmation that all of the existing smoke detectors and carbon monoxide detectors are installed in the right locations. However, we discovered that the existing units are past their 10 lifespan, and we recommend them to be replaced asap. All other devices in the home were tested and functioning properly prior to leaving today.

We provided options to remedy all of our electrical recommendations, which was presented today. The standard electrical package was approved by Matt and was partially completed today. We installed two brand new single pole switches in the master bedroom to replace the existing units that were failed/broken. We will return to rough in the new homeowner supplied light fixture on the staircase wall at a later date. The new switches were tested and working properly prior to leaving today.All of the options that were not approved will be emailed along with the electrical evaluation form and invoice for today’s visit. We thank you for allowing us in your home to service you and we look forward to servicing you in the future.

10 major benefits of reverse osmosis
1. Removes harmful contaminants
Can reduce lead, arsenic, fluoride, nitrates, and other dissolved contaminants, depending on the system.
2. Improves taste and odor
Reduces chlorine, dissolved solids, and other substances that can affect the taste and smell of drinking water.

4. Provides cleaner drinking water
Helps reduce exposure to certain contaminants in tap or well water.

Cleaner-tasting water can improve the flavor of coffee, tea, soups, and other foods.
6. Reduces water hardness
Removes some calcium and magnesium, helping reduce mineral buildup.

An under-sink RO system provides filtered water directly from a dedicated faucet.
8. Reduces bottled water consumption
Can save money and reduce plastic bottle waste.

Technician performed water quality testing and found the home’s water hardness to be 22 grains per gallon (GPG) and the ph level to be 8.0 ppm. A hardness level of 22 GPG is considered hard water and can lead to calcium and magnesium scale buildup inside water heaters, plumbing fixtures, faucets, shower heads, and water-using appliances. Over time, this mineral buildup can reduce appliance efficiency, shorten equipment life expectancy, cause spotting on dishes and glassware, and leave soap residue on fixtures and surfaces. The presence of chlorine, while common in municipal water supplies, can contribute to dry skin and hair and may deteriorate rubber seals and gaskets within the plumbing system over time.

To improve water quality and help protect the home’s plumbing system, technician recommends installing a City Soft water treatment system. The system is designed to soften the water by removing the hardness minerals that cause scale buildup while also reducing chlorine levels throughout the home. Benefits of the system include improved soap and detergent performance, reduced spotting and scaling, softer-feeling water, and increased protection and efficiency of plumbing fixtures and water-using appliances.

The proposed installation location for the City Soft system is near the existing pressure tank to allow for efficient integration into the home’s main water distribution system. The softener’s backwash drain lines will be routed and connected to the existing main drain located behind the water heater. An outlet is provided. Once installed, the system will provide conditioned water to the entire home and help minimize the long-term effects of hard water and chlorine exposure on the plumbing system.

10 major benefits of a water softener
1. Protects plumbing: Reduces mineral buildup inside pipes, faucets and showerheads.
2. Extends appliance life: Helps protect dishwashers, washing machines, water heaters and other appliances from scale buildup.
3. Improves water heater efficiency: Reduces mineral deposits that can interfere with heat transfer and increase energy consumption.
4. Softer skin: Many people notice less dry or tight-feeling skin after showering.
5. Softer hair: Can help reduce mineral residue that makes hair feel dry or dull.
6. Cleaner dishes and glassware: Helps prevent white spots and cloudy mineral deposits.
7. Less soap and detergent: Soft water allows soaps and detergents to work more effectively.
8. Cleaner showers and bathrooms: Reduces hard-water scale on shower doors, tubs and fixtures.
9. Softer laundry: Clothes and towels may feel softer and detergents can work more effectively.
10. Less cleaning and maintenance: Reduces time spent scrubbing mineral deposits from fixtures and surfaces.

e.439774781:
Premium Whole-Home Surge Protection
LPH will install a premium whole-home surge protection device at the home’s main electrical panel. This device is designed to protect the home’s electrical system and connected equipment from damaging voltage spikes and transient surges before they can travel throughout the home’s wiring.
Many homeowners think of lightning when they hear the term “surge,” but the majority of power surges actually originate inside the home. Everyday appliances such as air conditioners, refrigerators, heat pumps, furnaces, microwaves, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and even garage door openers create small electrical surges—known as microsurges—every time their motors cycle on and off. While each individual surge is small, thousands of these microsurges occur over time and gradually wear down the sensitive electronic components found in today’s modern appliances and equipment.
Whole-home surge protection helps absorb and divert these surges away from the home’s electrical system, reducing cumulative damage to expensive electronics and appliances. This is especially important in newer homes, where nearly every major appliance contains sophisticated circuit boards and microprocessors that are far more sensitive to voltage fluctuations than older equipment.
In addition to protecting against internally generated microsurges, whole-home surge protection also provides a critical first line of defense against larger surges originating from the utility company, switching events on the electrical grid, nearby lightning strikes, or power being restored after an outage.
Benefits of premium whole-home surge protection include:
	• Protects HVAC systems, refrigerators, ovens, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and other major appliances.
	• Helps safeguard sensitive electronics such as televisions, computers, gaming systems, networking equipment, and smart home devices.
	• Reduces the long-term effects of everyday microsurges that slowly degrade electronic components.
	• Can help extend the service life of modern appliances and equipment by reducing electrical stress on internal circuit boards.
	• Helps minimize the likelihood of costly repairs or premature equipment replacement due to surge damage.
	• Provides continuous protection for the entire home’s electrical system without relying solely on individual plug-in surge strips.
	• Offers added peace of mind during storms, utility switching events, and unexpected power outages.
As homes continue to rely on more connected technology and electronically controlled appliances, whole-home surge protection has become one of the most valuable upgrades for preserving the reliability, longevity, and performance of a home’s electrical equipment.

Premium Surge Protection Warranty & Replacement Coverage

The installed surge protection device also provides additional protection beyond the device itself. If the surge protector is ever sacrificed or fails as a result of a covered surge event, the device is backed by a lifetime warranty and coverage of up to $100,000 toward covered damage to the home’s electrical components and connected equipment, subject to the manufacturer’s warranty terms and conditions.

If the surge protector ever needs to be replaced under the warranty, the replacement device is provided at no charge. LPH will also handle the replacement installation for a $150 labor charge, helping make future warranty replacement straightforward and affordable for the homeowner.

This means the homeowner is not simply purchasing a surge protector—they are adding a long-term layer of protection to the home’s electrical system while also having manufacturer-backed coverage in the event of a significant surge.

As homes continue to rely on more connected technology and electronically controlled appliances, whole-home surge protection has become one of the most valuable upgrades for preserving the reliability, longevity, and performance of a home’s electrical equipment.

During today’s electrical system check, LPH performed a thorough evaluation of the home’s electrical system. This included inspecting the electrical panel, breakers, internal connections, grounding and bonding, and overall condition of the electrical service. We also checked receptacles and switches throughout the home, verified proper operation, looked for loose connections, signs of overheating, arcing, corrosion, and physical damage, and evaluated GFCI protection in the areas where required. We also reviewed the exterior electrical devices for proper weather protection and checked the smoke alarm protection throughout the home.

Summary of Findings & Recommendations:

During our evaluation, LPH identified the following items that we reviewed with the homeowner and provided options for:

1. Exterior Receptacles: Three exterior receptacles were identified for replacement with weather-resistant GFCI devices. Two existing devices are showing internal corrosion, while the third receptacle serving the outdoor hot tub is currently neither GFCI-protected nor weather-rated. LPH recommends replacing all three, properly mounting them to their electrical boxes, and sealing around the exterior to help prevent moisture intrusion.
2. Smoke Alarm: LPH recommends installing a new 10-year sealed-lithium-battery smoke alarm in the hallway outside the bedrooms to provide reliable smoke detection without the need for routine battery replacements.
3. Premium Whole-Home Surge Protection: LPH recommends installing our premium whole-home surge protection device at the electrical panel. This provides an additional layer of protection against damaging voltage spikes and surges that can affect sensitive electronics, appliances, and HVAC equipment throughout the home.
4. Bathroom Switch & Wiring Correction: LPH identified an existing bathroom switch that is arcing and should be replaced. Since the bathroom heater is no longer being used, LPH recommended removing the heater wiring from the switch configuration and installing a new twin single-pole switch to independently operate the fan and lighting. We also identified an improper wiring arrangement at the bathroom fan where the equipment grounding conductor was being used as a neutral due to insufficient conductors. LPH recommended correcting this wiring so the neutral is returned to its intended function and the equipment grounding conductor is properly reconnected.

Work Approved & Completed Today:

The homeowner elected to move forward with the bathroom wiring correction at this time. LPH completed the wiring repair, corrected the improper use of the grounding conductor, restored the neutral to its intended function, and properly reconnected the equipment ground. The bathroom fan and lighting controls were tested following the repair and confirmed to be functioning properly.

The remaining recommendations were reviewed with the homeowner for future consideration.

Today’s work was completed and tested. The invoice summary will be emailed to the homeowner for their records.

Thank you for allowing LPH into your home. It was a pleasure working with you, and we look forward to servicing you again in the future!

Heating System Inspection Findings & Recommendations

LPH completed a heating system inspection on the approximately 20-year-old standard gas furnace. At the time of inspection, the furnace was operational and producing heat. However, I identified several concerns worth addressing as we head into the heating season.

Inspection Findings:

1. System Efficiency: The furnace is currently operating at approximately 79% efficiency. While the system is still functioning, this efficiency level is not ideal compared to newer, more energy-efficient equipment. Replacing the system could provide improved efficiency and potentially lower energy costs.
2. System Cleaning: The furnace was found to be dirty. LPH recommends performing a professional system cleaning to help improve airflow, maintain proper system performance, and reduce the risk of premature component failure.
3. UV Bulb Replacement: The UV light bulbs are due for replacement. The manufacturer recommends replacing these bulbs every two years to maintain optimal performance.
4. Heat Exchanger Condition: During the inspection, I observed a significant amount of rust on the heat exchanger. Over time, corrosion can worsen and potentially lead to cracks or holes in the heat exchanger. If this occurs, the furnace could become unsafe to operate and may need to be shut down.

Recommendations:

LPH recommends addressing the maintenance items, including a professional furnace cleaning and UV bulb replacement. Additionally, due to the system’s age, current efficiency, and visible rust on the heat exchanger, we strongly recommend scheduling a Comfort Consultant to evaluate the system and provide replacement options.

With a 20-year-old furnace heading into another heating season, it’s important to consider the reliability of the equipment and the potential for unexpected breakdowns.

Overall Assessment:

The furnace is currently operational; however, given its age and the concerns identified during the inspection, LPH recommends considering replacement rather than continuing to invest in an aging system. Our goal is to help ensure you have a safe, reliable, and efficient heating system to get you through the upcoming winter.

Technician found error code 71 displayed on the control panel of the existing Rinnai CX199i tankless water heater. Technician removed the unit’s cover and discovered corrosion around the bypass tee. Technician cleaned the flame rods on the heat exchanger and restarted the tankless water heater; however, error code 71 remained displayed.

Technician contacted Rinnai technical support and worked through the diagnostic process to evaluate the unit’s control board and error code history. The recorded error history showed the following codes: 1-11, 2-11, 3-72, 4-72, 5-71, and 6-71. Following the diagnostic procedure, error code 71 did not return.

According to Rinnai technical support, error code 71 indicates a solenoid valve circuit failure or a potential control board failure. Moisture inside the unit can sometimes contribute to these issues. During further inspection of the bypass tee, technician identified that the water leak was originating from the elbow connected to the heat exchanger.

Rinnai technical support will ship a replacement heat exchanger, bypass tee, and new O-rings to Lancaster Plumbing and Heating (LPH). Once the replacement materials arrive, LPH will contact the owner to schedule a follow-up appointment to replace the affected components and address the leak.

This would allow the water to be softened before entering the water heaters and throughout the hot-water distribution system, helping reduce mineral buildup, scale accumulation, and potential damage to the water heaters, piping, and plumbing fixtures over time.
To incorporate the new commercial water softener, the technician would need to shut down the water supply to the hot-water system and reconfigure the existing 2-inch piping to properly accommodate the new equipment. This would require modifying the existing piping layout to direct the water through the softener before supplying the water heaters and distributing hot water throughout the building. Hot water service would be interrupted for the duration of the installation until all piping modifications and connections are completed and the system is returned to service.
The water softener's backwash drain would be connected to the existing 3-inch floor drain located near the backflow preventer to provide a proper discharge location during the regeneration cycle. An approved electrician would also need to install a dedicated electrical outlet for the new commercial water softener to provide the required power for the control valve and automatic regeneration cycles. i.437223277:
This afternoon I arrived at the Radanovic family home to conduct their annual electrical system and safety check. Upon my arrival Mrs. Radanovic informed me that her husband had mentioned that water sometimes seem to enter the home around the breaker panel, and their belief is that the rain water tracks down the main service wire where it then is deposited on and around the panel. My immediate action was to go and see if I could identify any weak points in the weather proofing that was performed when this service was installed 8 years ago in May of 2018. 

Upon approaching the meterbase I noticed that PPL had never attached one of their security locks on the meterbase locking hinge. I took this as an opportunity to see if there were any leaks allowing water to the internal portion of the meterbase when I noticed what became the primary focus of today’s visit. I found that one of the main power feeds phase cables had a rather large burn mark immediately where the bare conductor meets its fastening lug. I spent ample time trying to find a root cause of this burn, and asking Mrs. Radanovic questions regarding any past power outages, or if there seems to be any abnormal electrical behavior in the home. Mrs. Radanovic informed me that the only electrical mishap was regarding the massive storm the area was hit by in July of this year which caused them to experience 3 days of power loss. I was able to confirm that the phase was not actively 1.) melting nor 2.) burning/ overheating (see attached video). 

It appears as though the burn mark came from a one time event, such as a massive surge from the sudden re-energizing of the homes main power supply. I was also able to identify what seems to be rather progressive sun damage to the main cables sheathing on the exterior of the home, causing a scaly, sandpaper like texture on the service wire. I did the best I could to reweatherize and properly seal any area on the cable that seemed to me as a potential weak point for water to access. As far as the burn mark goes, I did not see any reason at this time to perform any kind of emergency replacements or mitigation, as all power levels are adequate in the home, and I found no continued signs of overheating or resistance. I have taken several pictures of the damage to the wire, and will use these photos as a means of monitoring potential further deterioration as we continue to come back and perform our annual system and safety checks. 

As for today, I had no recommendations for the Radanovic family and all systems appear to be in proper and functional condition. If you begin to notice any massive spikes in your electric bill ($100+), any strange behavior of your electrical systems, or become at all concerned about your homes electrical function moving forward, please do not hesitate to contact us. If you would like to schedule a time to speak with me regarding today’s findings in your absence, please feel free to call and I can coordinate a time where we can speak over the phone. Otherwise, thank you for having me out to your home today and I look forward to our next visit!

i.437325784:
Performed triple system checks on 3 20+ year old Payne, Bryant, and Carrier gas furnaces. At this time 1/3 of the units are operating properly and within spec. It should be duly noted that all three units are showing their age, however. The units for both the “break room” and “office” are both off at this time due to concerns about heat exchanger integrity and burning safety. 

The unit (Carrier) for the breakroom has what appears to be severe rusting on the outside of the primary heat exchanger. Given this is a horizontal application, it is unlikely that the evaporator coil is dripping onto the heat exchanger and causing exterior rust. Instead, it is my worry that the heat exchanger is rusting from the inside out. This is a safety concern. The unit is burning “cleanly” but any leakage on the heat exchanger will release CO into the conditioned space (which is bad). 

The unit covering the front offices has excessive CO coming off of the flue (>400 ppm air free). Due to this, it is shutoff. Though the integrity of the heat exchanger appears to be solid, the excessively high CO could cause a catastrophic problem if it were to develop a crack, and it is against code to keep it running at current combustion readings. Additionally, the gas valve appears to have gone bad as it is not holding steady pressure. This is probably unrelated to the high CO present in the flue; however, it is not helping and would be a pricey repair on a 20+ year old unit (if possible). 

I will be strongly recommending replacing both units for the breakroom and office, and would like to discuss finding on the warehouse unit with management. Additionally, I will be providing options to replace the UV lights for both the office and breakroom systems. If we do go with repair (please don’t), all furnaces would need in depth cleanings. Assuming we’re going to peruse replacement, I will write an option just to clean the unit in the warehouse. 

That being said, the work that was performed today involved changing all premium filters on the units and cleaning the evaporator coil on the warehouse unit. Additionally Larry spoke to me about the energy bill for the summer. Though I did not check the outdoor coils today, nothing I could see on the heating side of things appear to be causing higher energy consumption. My recommendation would be to reevaluate the cooling systems before summer proper starts to make sure they’re ready to go and no surprises have appeared from the last time they were check until now.

Came out today for a no heat on a 13 year old Amana. We had installed a new AC with new Honeywell communicating thermostat, and tenant believed that was the problem. Upon arrival, thermostat was blank. Found that the furnace control board was errored out on a blown fuse or flame rollout code. Flame rollout was tripped and upon reset furnace started back up. All thermostat connections were proper and thermostat operates properly when flame rollout was reset. 

Did a thorough visual inspection of the unit and all components that may have attributed to flame rollout. Performed a heating system check and found several areas of concerns with the heat exchanger. Ultimately we had way greater than 400 ppm of CO coming off of the flue so I condemned the heat exchanger. Talked to Sean about replacing the heat exchanger or getting the unit replaced. Sean elected to have a comfort consultant come out today so that he could make a decision on whether he will replace or repair. 

Please refer to system evaluation form for pictures and measurements taken. 

Waiving dispatch fee for this visit.
