i.437747187: Tech  was dispatched today to investigate a musty odor coming from the upstairs bathroom. Upon arrival, the technician was unable to detect any noticeable odors. As part of the inspection, the technician thoroughly cleaned all drain overflows, including the bathtub and bathroom vanity, to eliminate the possibility of odor coming from buildup within the overflows. The technician then asked the homeowner not to run any water while monitoring the water meter for approximately 30 minutes. During this time, there was no movement on the meter, indicating no active water usage or apparent leaks from dripping fixture. Tech ran all bathroom drains for approximately 10 minutes while inspecting the surrounding areas and drywall. No signs of active leaking or dripping were observed. At this time, the technician recommends having a professional water restoration company inspect the area to determine whether there may be hidden moisture or mold growth behind the drywall. The technician also explained that the toilet could potentially be contributing to the odor. Possible causes include a deteriorated wax ring or an issue with the toilet flange, which may allow sewer odors to escape. The technician was on-site for approximately two hours. No diagnostic fee was charged due to the homeowner’s concerns regarding the diagnostic charge. Thank you for trusting LPH with your plumbing needs!

e.438464168: Homeowner has a complaint about a musty smell in the bathroom upstairs. Technician ruled everything out, and the toilet wax seal could potentially be giving that smell. That wax seal could be deteriorating or there could be an issue with the toilet flange. Technician cannot promise this will fix the issue. Technician would pull toilet and install new wax seal. Depending on the condition of the toilet flange further charges may apply.

i.437752903:
Out to home today for the yearly plumbing inspection. Upon arrival to home, there was only one concern to note. They have noticed that there is moisture buildup behind the current water softener system. Evaluated unit and found system to dripping from discharge piping when on standby mode. Due to age of system, suggested best solution is to replace the water treatment system. In the meantime, unplugged the unit and bypassed the softener to prevent further leakage. 

From there, performed full home plumbing inspection today. Inspected and evaluated 11 year old water heater system. Observed corrosion and moisture at the cold side inlet to the system. System is within the end of its average lifespan of 8-12 years. Due to current issues and age of system, suggested replacement to prevent further leakage and reliable hot water. Performed water quality test and found high hardness and chlorine in the water. For both major contaminants, suggested installation of our CitySoft Water filtration system to remove both hardness and chlorine through use of its dual-bed system. Lastly, tested water pressure to verify a safe threshold inside the home. 

Only other concern found during today’s evaluation has to do with the kitchen faucet. Found that the faucet is coming loose and no longer swivels at the base as intended. Current faucet is also extremely low-end. Suggested replacement for a higher quality moen faucet. Provided options for replacement of fixture in both pull-out and pull-down spray units. 

Went over recommendations with homeowners relatives who were onsite today. Emailed all recommendations to homeowners. Pricing provided today is valid for 60 days. If there are any questions about our recommendations, please reach out to our office. Thank you for trusting LPH.

I also inspected the main electrical panel to rule out any additional electrical issues. All breakers were receiving acceptable voltage readings, all connections were secure, and there were no visible signs of overheating or damage.

While on site, I also evaluated the sunroom ceiling fan and provided an estimate for a future replacement. An installation option was provided for a customer-supplied ceiling fan.

I was out today to discuss options for replacing the homeowners’ current HVAC system with a newer, more energy-efficient system.

During our conversation, the homeowners mentioned they are preparing to leave for Florida for the winter and will be away for approximately five months. While reviewing their existing heat pump, we discussed that the dual capacitor is nearing the limits of its operating specifications. I explained that if the capacitor fails, it could prevent the heat pump from starting and operating properly while they are away, potentially leaving the home without heat.

At this time, the homeowners are primarily interested in gathering pricing for a future system replacement. I reviewed the benefits of upgrading to a new system, including improved energy efficiency, all-new equipment, a 10-year parts warranty, and a 10-year labor warranty. We also discussed the benefits of a Wi-Fi thermostat, which would allow them to remotely monitor and control their HVAC system while they are in Florida, providing additional peace of mind.

After reviewing everything, the homeowners decided they would prefer to hold off on replacing the system for now and requested that all options be emailed over for their review.

I left my business card with my contact information and encouraged them to call or text me with any questions or concerns.

Thank you again for allowing me into your home today and giving me the opportunity to go over your HVAC replacement options. I look forward to working with you when the time is right.

Today I was called out to address several concerns at the home. The homeowner requested that all openings be sealed to help prevent critters from entering the property. She also reported experiencing intermittent power issues.

I inspected all electrical connections at the panel, meter base, and transfer switch. All connections appeared to be in good condition. However, I noticed the meter base is slowly pulling away from the wall due to ground settling. I recommended installing a slip riser to prevent future stress or damage to the meter base and service connections.

All voltage readings were within acceptable ranges.

The homeowner also reported that the pond pump had been tripping the breaker intermittently. I inspected the breaker and associated outlets but did not find any apparent issues. I advised the homeowner to unplug the pump during the next rain event to determine whether the issue is being caused by the pump itself or potentially damaged wiring along the circuit.

Due to the reported power issues, I also recommended installing whole-home surge protection to help protect the home’s electrical equipment and appliances from potential voltage surges. The homeowner declined the recommendation at this time due to cost and chose to hold off until next year.

All requested openings were sealed, and the invoice was emailed to the homeowner.

Findings and Recommendations:

During today’s evaluation, we identified an opportunity to improve the circuit separation for the sump pump and water softener. Both appliances were currently spliced into the living room GFCI circuit through a junction box located beside the electrical panel. Sharing this circuit can contribute to nuisance GFCI tripping and potentially interrupt power to the sump pump and water softener when the living room circuit experiences an issue.

* Garage GFCI Protection: Install a new GFCI receptacle in the garage to provide additional protection against electrical shock.
* Whole-Home Surge Protection: Install a whole-home surge protection device at the electrical panel to help protect appliances, electronics, and sensitive equipment from damaging voltage spikes caused by utility fluctuations, lightning, and everyday operation of larger electrical equipment.

Completed Work:

e.438790197:
Premium Whole-Home Surge Protection
LPH will install a premium whole-home surge protection device at the home’s main electrical panel. This device is designed to protect the home’s electrical system and connected equipment from damaging voltage spikes and transient surges before they can travel throughout the home’s wiring.
Many homeowners think of lightning when they hear the term “surge,” but the majority of power surges actually originate inside the home. Everyday appliances such as air conditioners, refrigerators, heat pumps, furnaces, microwaves, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and even garage door openers create small electrical surges—known as microsurges—every time their motors cycle on and off. While each individual surge is small, thousands of these microsurges occur over time and gradually wear down the sensitive electronic components found in today’s modern appliances and equipment.
Whole-home surge protection helps absorb and divert these surges away from the home’s electrical system, reducing cumulative damage to expensive electronics and appliances. This is especially important in newer homes, where nearly every major appliance contains sophisticated circuit boards and microprocessors that are far more sensitive to voltage fluctuations than older equipment.
In addition to protecting against internally generated microsurges, whole-home surge protection also provides a critical first line of defense against larger surges originating from the utility company, switching events on the electrical grid, nearby lightning strikes, or power being restored after an outage.
Benefits of premium whole-home surge protection include:
	• Protects HVAC systems, refrigerators, ovens, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and other major appliances.
	• Helps safeguard sensitive electronics such as televisions, computers, gaming systems, networking equipment, and smart home devices.
	• Reduces the long-term effects of everyday microsurges that slowly degrade electronic components.
	• Can help extend the service life of modern appliances and equipment by reducing electrical stress on internal circuit boards.
	• Helps minimize the likelihood of costly repairs or premature equipment replacement due to surge damage.
	• Provides continuous protection for the entire home’s electrical system without relying solely on individual plug-in surge strips.
	• Offers added peace of mind during storms, utility switching events, and unexpected power outages.
As homes continue to rely on more connected technology and electronically controlled appliances, whole-home surge protection has become one of the most valuable upgrades for preserving the reliability, longevity, and performance of a home’s electrical equipment.

Premium Surge Protection Warranty & Replacement Coverage

The installed surge protection device also provides additional protection beyond the device itself. If the surge protector is ever sacrificed or fails as a result of a covered surge event, the device is backed by a lifetime warranty and coverage of up to $100,000 toward covered damage to the home’s electrical components and connected equipment, subject to the manufacturer’s warranty terms and conditions.

If the surge protector ever needs to be replaced under the warranty, the replacement device is provided at no charge. LPH will also handle the replacement installation for a $150 labor charge, helping make future warranty replacement straightforward and affordable for the homeowner.

This means the homeowner is not simply purchasing a surge protector—they are adding a long-term layer of protection to the home’s electrical system while also having manufacturer-backed coverage in the event of a significant surge.

As homes continue to rely on more connected technology and electronically controlled appliances, whole-home surge protection has become one of the most valuable upgrades for preserving the reliability, longevity, and performance of a home’s electrical equipment.

i.438645175:
During today’s electrical system check, LPH performed an evaluation of the home’s electrical system, including the main electrical panel, breakers, visible wiring and connections, grounding and bonding, receptacles, switches, GFCI protection, exterior electrical devices, smoke detectors, and general electrical safety throughout the home. We also reviewed the overall condition and age of the existing electrical equipment and discussed potential improvements to the home’s electrical safety, reliability, and functionality.

GFCI Protection & Electrical Safety

We reviewed several areas throughout the home where GFCI protection is important, particularly the kitchen countertop receptacles, as well as other locations such as the washing machine receptacle and other areas where protection is required. GFCI devices are designed to quickly interrupt power when they detect an electrical current imbalance, helping reduce the risk of electrical shock, especially in areas where water and electricity may come into contact.

Exterior Receptacles & Weather Protection

We discussed the importance of having properly weather-rated electrical devices and enclosures at all exterior locations. One existing exterior GFCI located on the outside wall of the garage was found tripped, with evidence of water intrusion being a concern. The existing gray exterior cover is not properly rated for the exposed location and does not provide the necessary protection against direct weather exposure. Proper weather-resistant GFCI devices and appropriately rated in-use covers help protect electrical connections from rain and moisture, reducing the potential for corrosion, nuisance tripping, and premature device failure.

Back-Stabbed Electrical Devices

We also reviewed locations throughout the home where receptacles and switches were originally wired using the back-stab connection method. These connections rely on internal spring tension to hold the wiring in place rather than the more secure screw-terminal connections. Over time, these connections can lose their holding tension, potentially allowing wires to loosen. Loose connections can create electrical resistance, excessive heat, intermittent operation, and potentially electrical arcing or damage to the devices. We explained why upgrading these devices to properly secured connections can help improve long-term reliability and reduce the potential for overheating.

Smoke & Carbon Monoxide Detection

We discussed adding an additional smoke detector for the downstairs bedroom to provide appropriate detection and notification in that sleeping area. We also reviewed the option of upgrading the existing smoke detectors to newer 10-year sealed-battery models. These units eliminate the need for routine battery replacements every couple of years and provide a convenient long-term solution for maintaining smoke detection throughout the home.

The homeowner stated that they are comfortable handling the GFCI replacements, exterior receptacles, back-stabbed device replacements, and smoke detector improvements themselves at this time.

Electrical Panel Replacement – 200-Amp GE Panel

LPH discussed the age of the existing 200-amp GE electrical panel, which is approximately 41 years old. Although the panel currently shows no visible rust or corrosion, it has exceeded the typical recommended service life of approximately 25–40 years.

We explained how internal breaker components, bus connections, and connection points experience wear over time. Aging components can contribute to loose connections, inconsistent breaker operation, overheating, and potential electrical arcing. e.438882972:
Premium Whole-Home Surge Protection
LPH will install a premium whole-home surge protection device at the home’s main electrical panel. This device is designed to protect the home’s electrical system and connected equipment from damaging voltage spikes and transient surges before they can travel throughout the home’s wiring.
Many homeowners think of lightning when they hear the term “surge,” but the majority of power surges actually originate inside the home. Everyday appliances such as air conditioners, refrigerators, heat pumps, furnaces, microwaves, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and even garage door openers create small electrical surges—known as microsurges—every time their motors cycle on and off. While each individual surge is small, thousands of these microsurges occur over time and gradually wear down the sensitive electronic components found in today’s modern appliances and equipment.
Whole-home surge protection helps absorb and divert these surges away from the home’s electrical system, reducing cumulative damage to expensive electronics and appliances. This is especially important in newer homes, where nearly every major appliance contains sophisticated circuit boards and microprocessors that are far more sensitive to voltage fluctuations than older equipment.
In addition to protecting against internally generated microsurges, whole-home surge protection also provides a critical first line of defense against larger surges originating from the utility company, switching events on the electrical grid, nearby lightning strikes, or power being restored after an outage.
Benefits of premium whole-home surge protection include:
	• Protects HVAC systems, refrigerators, ovens, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and other major appliances.
	• Helps safeguard sensitive electronics such as televisions, computers, gaming systems, networking equipment, and smart home devices.
	• Reduces the long-term effects of everyday microsurges that slowly degrade electronic components.
	• Can help extend the service life of modern appliances and equipment by reducing electrical stress on internal circuit boards.
	• Helps minimize the likelihood of costly repairs or premature equipment replacement due to surge damage.
	• Provides continuous protection for the entire home’s electrical system without relying solely on individual plug-in surge strips.
	• Offers added peace of mind during storms, utility switching events, and unexpected power outages.
As homes continue to rely on more connected technology and electronically controlled appliances, whole-home surge protection has become one of the most valuable upgrades for preserving the reliability, longevity, and performance of a home’s electrical equipment.

The installed surge protection device also provides additional protection beyond the device itself. If the surge protector is ever sacrificed or fails as a result of a covered surge event, the device is backed by a lifetime warranty and coverage of up to $100,000 toward covered damage to the home’s electrical components and connected equipment, subject to the manufacturer’s warranty terms and conditions.

If the surge protector ever needs to be replaced under the warranty, the replacement device is provided at no charge. LPH will also handle the replacement installation for a $150 labor charge, helping make future warranty replacement straightforward and affordable for the homeowner.

This means the homeowner is not simply purchasing a surge protector—they are adding a long-term layer of protection to the home’s electrical system while also having manufacturer-backed coverage in the event of a significant surge.

As homes continue to rely on more connected technology and electronically controlled appliances, whole-home surge protection has become one of the most valuable upgrades for preserving the reliability, longevity, and performance of a home’s electrical equipment.

Performed heating system check on propane furnace. Please we attached evaluation form for system readings and photos. I adjusted propane pressures due to incoming being lower than furnace requirements. We also had the unit going off on high temperature limit after 10 to 15 minutes of run time. It is suspected that this is caused by the return coming into the back of the furnace and the higher outdoor temperature of the combustion air. We discussed cleaning the furnace since the blower has a dust layer and the burners are very rusty. 

As I was about to leave the customer informed me that they smelled gas from the furnace. I checked with the leak detector and found the vent tower on the furnace gas valve was leaking propane. Customer approved replacement of gas valve. I set manifold pressures to manufacturer specs and double checked propane pressure and lockup pressure (11.6 inWC standing, 12.14 inWC lockup). No further leaks detected. Burners were cleaned during today’s repair.

Smoke Detector Replacements:

LPH installed four new 10-year sealed lithium battery smoke detectors throughout the home. Additionally, one existing hardwired smoke detector was replaced with a new hardwired smoke detector equipped with battery backup. One hardwired combination smoke and carbon monoxide detector with battery backup was also installed. These replacements provide updated detection equipment and reliable early-warning protection in the event of a fire or carbon monoxide emergency.

Master Bathroom Exhaust Fan Replacement:

LPH removed and replaced the existing exhaust fan in the master bathroom. The original fan was noticeably noisy, and the motor had begun making a knocking sound, indicating signs of mechanical wear. The new fan was installed to restore proper ventilation, reduce operating noise, and help remove excess moisture from the bathroom.

New Bedroom Receptacle Installation:

LPH removed the existing device box in the hallway and utilized the opening to access the existing wiring. An additional wire was installed from the existing electrical box through the wall to a new location on the opposite side, inside the bedroom. A new cut-in electrical box and standard duplex receptacle were installed at the new location. All electrical connections were properly secured, and the new receptacle was tested to verify proper operation.

All approved work was completed, and the newly installed devices and equipment were tested and verified to be functioning properly prior to leaving. The hot tub jet control button was also repaired and verified to be operating properly at no additional charge.

Today’s invoice summary will be emailed to the homeowner for their records.

Thank you for allowing LPH into your home. It was a pleasure working with you, and we look forward to servicing you again in the future!

Technician recommends scheduling routine maintenance on the Noritz tankless water heater. Routine maintenance includes flushing the heat exchanger to help remove mineral buildup, cleaning the flame rods, inspecting and cleaning the air intake screen, and cleaning the cold-water inlet filter. Regular maintenance helps maintain proper operation, improve efficiency, and extend the service life of the tankless water heater.

i.439213359: This afternoon I arrived at the Mihoci family home to analyze a refrigerator fault. Upon my arrival I found that upon opening the refrigerator doors the GFCI for the fridge would trip. I noted that the breaker for the panel appears to be in good condition and is allowing a proper 122 volts to be sent to the refrigerator outlet. After actuating the doors a couple of times I was able to deduce that the GFCI only appears to trip when the left door, the one with the flapper (articulating mullion) is opened. I was able to slowly open the door and it did not trip the GFCI. With both doors open, I manually actuated the mullion and it immediately tripped the GFCI receptacle. The flapper (mullion) has a small heating element within it, as well as several sets of communication wires connected to the other fridge components such as the sensor on the top that activates the light and the sensor which tells the fridge that the door is closed. I figure that since the GFCI only appears to trip when it is actuated, that there is probably a damaged or kinked wire in its hinges that is short circuiting when it is opened or closed. Otherwise there could be moisture within this portion of the appliance causing the trip. I encouraged Mr. Mihoci to contact an appliance repair shop such as Brubaker inc. on Harrisburg Pike, and or Sears Home Services. If you require any further electrical services, please do not hesitate to contact us. Thank you for having me out this afternoon and I look forward to our next visit!

i.439271336:
LPH responded to the home to investigate a reported hot, burning electrical smell coming from the basement. Upon arrival, we noticed a faint electrical burning odor as soon as we began descending the basement steps. We began a thorough investigation of the home’s electrical system, inspecting accessible junction boxes, electrical equipment, and appliances in an effort to identify the source of the smell.

During our investigation, we noticed a slight burnt motor odor coming from the dishwasher control panel. We also identified a much stronger burnt motor smell coming from the basement dehumidifier. Although the dehumidifier had reportedly not been operating for several days, turning the unit on caused the odor to become significantly stronger. The motor was visibly struggling, shuddering during operation, and producing several popping sounds. Based on these observations, the dehumidifier appears to have an internal motor or mechanical failure and should be replaced. Continued operation is not recommended.

Electrical Panel Findings:

When focusing our inspection on the home’s electrical panel, we immediately identified concerning evidence of previous water intrusion throughout the panel and multiple breakers. Visible conditions included:

* Rust buildup and corrosion around breaker screws, rivets, and other metal components.
* Dried water stains and mineral deposits that appeared to have pooled on top of breakers and traveled down their sides.
* Evidence of previous water accumulation along the bottom of the electrical panel.
* Corrosion and deterioration affecting multiple breaker components.
* Unusually rough connections when reinstalling several breakers onto the panel’s bus bar, suggesting that the breaker connection points may have been compromised by moisture and corrosion.

Although the bus bar itself did not show extensive visible corrosion, the condition of the affected breakers and their connection points is concerning. Corrosion and oxidation at electrical connection points can increase electrical resistance, creating unwanted heat buildup and potentially contributing to arcing or unreliable electrical connections.

We also noticed a slight internal overheating odor coming from some of the breakers during our inspection. While these findings are concerning and could potentially contribute to excessive heat within the electrical system, we cannot definitively identify the electrical panel as the source of the original burning smell reported in the basement.

LPH Recommendations:

Due to the visible water damage, corrosion, compromised breaker components, and questionable breaker-to-bus connections, LPH recommends addressing the electrical panel rather than continuing to operate it in its current condition.

We provided two options for the homeowner to review:

Option 1 – Complete Electrical Panel Replacement:
Replace the existing electrical panel with a new panel, including the necessary components and updates to bring the installation up to current applicable electrical code requirements. This option addresses the condition of the existing panel as a whole rather than simply replacing individual components that have already experienced water damage.

Option 2 – Complete Breaker Replacement:
Replace all existing breakers within the electrical panel due to the visible corrosion, water damage, and concerns surrounding their connection points. This option addresses the compromised breakers while retaining the existing panel and bus assembly. However, it does not eliminate the potential concerns associated with the existing panel itself.

Given the amount of water intrusion and deterioration observed, LPH’s professional recommendation is to proceed with the complete panel replacement. This provides the most comprehensive solution by replacing the affected electrical components and restoring dependable connections throughout the panel.

The homeowner was made aware of our findings and the two available options. We will provide the estimates along with today’s evaluation for review and consideration.

e.439555671:
Electrical Panel Replacement and Whole-Home Surge Protection

LPH recommends replacing the existing approximately 44- to 45-year-old electrical panel with a new premium 42-space Eaton CH electrical panel and installing whole-home surge protection.

The existing panel has been in service for several decades and is well beyond the typical service life of the equipment. As electrical components age, internal connections, bus bars, breakers, and terminations can deteriorate over time. This can increase the potential for overheating, poor electrical connections, nuisance breaker issues, and reduced reliability of the home’s electrical system.

Scope of Work Includes:

* Remove the existing electrical panel.
* Install a new premium 42-space Eaton CH load center.
* Transfer and properly terminate existing branch circuit wiring.
* Replace existing breakers with new, appropriately sized Eaton CH breakers.
* Install premium whole-home surge protection at the new electrical panel.
* Properly integrate and configure the surge protective device.
* Inspect accessible wiring and connections for signs of heat damage or deterioration.
* Properly label the new electrical panel and identify all branch circuits.
* Test the completed installation and verify proper operation.

Benefits of the Upgrade

The new 42-space Eaton CH panel will provide modern electrical distribution equipment with additional breaker capacity for the home’s existing and future electrical needs. This upgrade will improve electrical system organization, provide dependable circuit protection, and make future electrical maintenance and additions easier.

The whole-home surge protective device will help protect sensitive electronics, appliances, HVAC equipment, and other connected devices against damaging voltage surges caused by lightning, utility disturbances, and everyday electrical events.

Peace-of-Mind Warranty

Your new Eaton CH electrical panel and associated breakers are protected by a 10-year parts and labor warranty while maintaining an active LPH Service Partner Plan (SPP) membership, subject to applicable warranty terms.

LPH Recommendation

Replacing the aging electrical panel and installing whole-home surge protection provides an important improvement to the home’s electrical infrastructure. Rather than continuing to rely on decades-old electrical equipment, this upgrade provides modern distribution equipment, additional circuit capacity, and added protection for the home’s electrical investments.

LPH recommends completing this upgrade to improve the overall reliability, safety, and long-term performance of the home’s electrical system.

e.439566114:
Complete 200 Amp Underground Electrical Service Replacement

This project includes a complete modernization of your home’s electrical service, upgrading the existing equipment to a reliable, high-capacity 200 Amp electrical system. This includes replacing the underground service components, exterior service equipment, interior electrical panel, breakers, and associated grounding and bonding components.

Scope of Work Includes:

* New 200 Amp meter base.
* New underground service entrance conductors.
* Replacement of existing underground service conduit and associated connections as required.
* New 200 Amp exterior emergency disconnect.
* New 200 Amp premium 42-space Eaton CH electrical panel.
* All new appropriately sized breakers throughout.
* Whole-home premium surge protection.
* Complete grounding and bonding system upgrade, including two grounding electrodes where required.
* Proper termination, labeling, and identification of all electrical circuits.
* All necessary permits, inspections, and PPL coordination.

Underground Service Protection

LPH will replace the existing underground service connections and associated conduit components as required to establish a properly protected and reliable electrical service. All underground service conductors will be installed in appropriate protective conduit, with properly secured connections and sealed entry points to help prevent moisture intrusion and protect the electrical service from environmental deterioration.

This installation helps protect the underground service conductors against physical damage, moisture exposure, and premature deterioration, providing a more dependable electrical connection for the home.

Interior Electrical Panel Replacement and Surge Protection

LPH will remove the existing approximately 44- to 45-year-old electrical panel and replace it with a new premium 42-space Eaton CH load center. As electrical equipment ages, internal components, bus connections, breakers, and terminations can deteriorate over time. This can increase the potential for overheating, poor electrical connections, nuisance breaker issues, and reduced reliability.

The new Eaton CH panel will provide modern electrical distribution equipment with additional breaker capacity for the home’s existing and future electrical needs. All existing branch circuits will be transferred and properly terminated with appropriately sized new breakers.

As part of this upgrade, LPH will install premium whole-home surge protection directly at the new electrical panel. This device helps protect sensitive electronics, appliances, and other connected equipment against damaging voltage surges caused by lightning, utility disturbances, and other electrical events.

Complete Grounding and Bonding Upgrade

LPH will install or upgrade the home’s grounding electrode system as required, including two grounding electrodes where required, properly sized grounding conductors, and bonding of applicable metal water piping and other qualifying metal systems.

An effective grounding and bonding system is an essential part of electrical safety. It provides a proper path for fault current and helps ensure protective devices operate as intended during an electrical fault.

Peace-of-Mind Warranty

Your new Eaton CH electrical panel and associated breakers are protected by a 10-year parts and labor warranty while maintaining an active LPH Service Partner Plan (SPP) membership, subject to applicable warranty terms.

Long-Term Reliability and Protection

This complete 200 Amp underground electrical service replacement will modernize the home’s electrical infrastructure from the underground service entrance through the interior distribution panel.

By replacing the aging service equipment, underground service components, panel, and breakers, while upgrading the grounding and bonding system and incorporating whole-home surge protection, LPH is providing a comprehensive improvement in electrical safety, reliability, and long-term performance.

The new 200 Amp system will also provide additional electrical capacity to accommodate the home’s existing demands and future electrical upgrades.

LPH recommends completing the entire service replacement rather than addressing only the interior panel. Replacing the underground service components and associated electrical equipment together provides a more complete solution and helps avoid leaving aging service components connected to brand-new interior equipment.

A pressure reducing valve (PRV) is a plumbing device that automatically lowers the water pressure coming into a home or building from the municipal water supply and keeps it at a safe, consistent level.

Why would someone install one?
There are several important reasons:
Protect plumbing pipes: Excessive water pressure puts unnecessary stress on pipes, joints, and fittings.
Prevent leaks: High pressure can contribute to leaking connections and premature plumbing failures.
Protect appliances: Water heaters, washing machines, dishwashers, refrigerators, and other fixtures can be damaged by excessive pressure.
Extend fixture lifespan: Faucets, toilets, shower valves, and other plumbing components last longer when pressure is controlled.
Reduce water waste: Excessive pressure can cause faucets and showerheads to use more water than necessary.
Reduce water hammer: Lowering excessive pressure can help reduce banging noises in plumbing, although water hammer may require a separate solution.

Installing a sediment filter near the pressure tank is also recommended to help protect the home’s plumbing system from debris coming from the well.

Well water commonly carries sand, silt, and other sediment that can enter the home’s plumbing system. By installing a sediment filter immediately after the pressure tank, the filter will capture these particles before the water continues through the rest of the home.

Benefits of installing a sediment filter include:
	•	Removing sand, silt, and debris coming from the well
	•	Protecting plumbing fixtures such as faucets, toilets, and shower valves from sediment buildup
	•	Preventing premature wear on appliances such as the water heater, washing machine, and treatment equipment
	•	Helping protect the Sanitizer Plus system by reducing the amount of sediment entering the unit

The sediment filter would be installed on the main water line near the pressure tank, allowing it to filter the water before it enters the home’s plumbing system and before it reaches the water treatment equipment.

This addition will help maintain cleaner water throughout the home and extend the life of plumbing fixtures and water treatment equipment.

Installing a UV light system near the pressure tank is also recommended to help protect the home’s drinking water from harmful bacteria that can sometimes be present in well water.

Private well systems are not treated by municipal facilities, so bacteria such as E. coli and other microorganisms can potentially enter the water supply. A UV disinfection system uses ultraviolet light to neutralize bacteria and other microorganisms as the water passes through the unit.

Benefits of installing a UV light system include:
	•	Eliminating harmful bacteria and microorganisms that may be present in well water
	•	Providing safe drinking water throughout the home
	•	Continuous disinfection without adding chemicals to the water
	•	Protecting the household’s health by ensuring the water supply remains sanitary

The UV light system would be installed on the main water line near the pressure tank, allowing the water to be disinfected before it enters the home’s plumbing system. This placement ensures that all water distributed throughout the home has been properly treated.

Adding a UV system, along with the sediment filter and Sanitizer Plus treatment system, will create a more complete well-water treatment setup that improves water quality, protects plumbing fixtures, and ensures a safe and healthy water supply for the home.

The existing Waterfall water softener is old and no longer operational. The home’s water supply is provided by a private well. Testing shows the water hardness is approximately 22 grains per gallon, which is considered very hard water. In addition, the water is highly acidic with a pH of 5.5, making it corrosive to plumbing components and fixtures over time. Acidic water can deteriorate copper piping, valves, fixtures, and appliances connected to the water system.

Due to the combination of high hardness, low pH (acidic water), and the potential presence of iron commonly found in well water, the technician highly recommends replacing the existing system with a Sanitizer Plus treatment system. This system is designed to treat multiple well-water issues simultaneously by:
	•	Softening the water to reduce hardness buildup in plumbing and fixtures
	•	Neutralizing acidic water to help prevent corrosion of piping and equipment
	•	Removing iron and other common well-water contaminants

The proposed Sanitizer Plus system would be installed near the water heater for optimal access to the home’s main water distribution.

Installation details are as follows:
	•	The inlet to the Sanitizer Plus will be connected to the main cold water supply line before the washing machine connection to ensure treated water is distributed throughout the home.
	•	The backwash drain line will be connected to the main drain line located above the installation area.
	•	A dedicated electrical outlet is already available near the installation location to power the system.

This installation will significantly improve overall water quality while protecting the home’s plumbing system from the damaging effects of hard and acidic well water.

In addition, the washing machine also discharges directly into the sump pump pit. This setup is not ideal and does not meet proper plumbing practices for handling greywater discharge.

The technician will remove the existing double-compartment concrete utility sink and replace it with a new utility sink and faucet. The new utility sink will be properly connected to a laundry pump system to ensure wastewater is discharged correctly.

Installation and modifications will include the following:
	•	The new utility sink drain will connect directly to the new laundry pump basin.
	•	The laundry pump discharge line will be piped to the main drain located above the installation area to properly remove wastewater from the pump basin.
	•	The laundry pump vent will be installed and terminated to the exterior through the side of the home above the washing machine to allow proper venting of the system.
	•	The technician will repipe a section of the main drain line to allow the laundry pump discharge to connect properly and to ensure the installation complies with International Plumbing Code (IPC) standards.
	•	Once installed, the washing machine will discharge into the new utility sink, which will then drain into the laundry pump basin.

An electrical outlet is already available near the installation area to power the laundry pump system.

This installation will provide a proper and code-compliant method of removing wastewater from the basement laundry area, preventing greywater from entering the sump system and improving the overall function and reliability of the drainage system.

Technician found a puddle of water on the garage floor near the chimney, approximately 3–4 feet away from the garage hose bib. Technician determined there are no other plumbing fixtures or water lines near the chimney, other than the plumbing located in the basement along the wall adjacent to the garage.

Technician inspected the basement plumbing and identified the water heater, hot and cold water supply lines, and the cold water line supplying the garage hose bib. Of the plumbing fixtures and water lines in this area, the garage hose bib was the only potential source that could account for the water accumulating near the chimney.

The water followed the path of least resistance toward the chimney and away from the garage door, consistent with the location of the puddle.

Based on these findings, technician believes the puddle may have been caused by the garage hose bib being left on, allowing water to travel across the garage floor and collect near the chimney. During the inspection, technician also noticed the hose bib has a slow drip, indicating a possible failure of the packing nut. This ongoing drip could also contribute to water accumulating in the same area.

Recommendation: Technician recommends replacing the existing garage hose bib to correct the slow drip and help prevent further water accumulation on the garage floor.

i.439618474:
Today, LPH was called out due to an issue with the lamppost circuit tripping the breaker.

Upon evaluation, I removed the switch to verify that it was not the cause of the issue. The breaker continued to trip. I then disconnected both the light fixture and GFCI, but the breaker continued to trip. This indicated that the issue was likely within the wiring.

After speaking with Mike, I was informed that there had been a previous splice in the mulch bed. We excavated the area, located the existing splice, and cut the wire at that location. After doing so, the breaker stopped tripping. I then installed a new splice, and the breaker held without tripping.

I informed Mike that, due to the deteriorated condition of the existing wiring, I strongly recommend replacing the entire wire run and PVC conduit to provide a reliable, long-term solution.

We also discussed the possibility of installing two additional Cadet switches: one to control the lamppost and another to control the front exterior light.

Mike advised that, for the time being, his preference is to have the existing wiring spliced and repaired rather than proceed with a complete replacement

Upon installing the splice kit we found there is a direct short which we didn’t see since we didn’t hook up ground to test. That section of wire wil need to be replaced. I provided several option to see what fits there needs. Emailed invoice.
